question.prompt: What is the remainder when \(2^{202} +202\) is divided by \(2^{101}+2^{51}+1?\)

solutions.title: Multiply by a matching factor
solutions.explanation:
The exponents satisfy \(2\cdot51=101+1\). This makes a difference of squares cancel the large middle terms.

Let
\[
m=2^{101}+2^{51}+1.
\]
Multiply \(m\) by the integer obtained by changing the sign of its \(2^{51}\) term:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m(2^{101}-2^{51}+1)
&=(2^{101}+1)^2-(2^{51})^2\\
&=2^{202}+2^{102}+1-2^{102}\\
&=2^{202}+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{202}+202
=m(2^{101}-2^{51}+1)+201.
\]
This writes the dividend as an integer multiple of the divisor plus \(201\). Since \(0\le201<m\), this is a valid remainder.

The remainder is \(\boxed{201}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

solutions.title: Square a congruence
solutions.explanation:
The divisor gives a simpler expression for \(2^{101}\) when working with remainders. Squaring that expression reaches \(2^{202}\) directly.

Let \(m=2^{101}+2^{51}+1\). We write \(u\equiv v\pmod m\) when \(u-v\) is divisible by \(m\). From the definition of \(m\),
\[
2^{101}\equiv-(2^{51}+1)\pmod m.
\]
We may square this congruence: replacing a number by another differing by a multiple of \(m\) changes its square only by a multiple of \(m\), as expansion shows. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{202}
&\equiv(2^{51}+1)^2\\
&=2^{102}+2^{52}+1\\
&=2(2^{101}+2^{51}+1)-1\\
&=2m-1\\
&\equiv-1\pmod m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding \(202\) gives
\[
2^{202}+202\equiv201\pmod m.
\]
Since \(201\) is nonnegative and smaller than \(m\), the remainder is \(\boxed{201}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
